name: Aaron Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day sound like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a folk string band, play mandolin, write practice parts and teach three new players. I have a master's degree in music and thirty-two years of paid festivals behind me; the younger band members ask me to settle the tune when it races. I like watching a shy player take the melody at a dance.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Does leading the band bring a steady wage?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner does seasonal shifts at a garden centre and our children are grown. Our regional festival pays a low leader fee for a short season, and there are few similar bands near us. We rent and have three weeks of expenses saved. I use AI now and then for draft travel lists after other musicians try it, but check each stop against the signed schedule.

I'd say the **mandolin tune** still follows dancers' turns.
think: Our **three-week reserve** and short festival season expose winter rent.
My partner's **seasonal pay** cannot fill a cancelled set.
do: Confirm **five paid sets** and three pupils; request written cancellation and mileage fees.
Check **AI travel drafts** against bookings and save fifth of extra cleared dance fees after essentials toward one month.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary seasonal pay gaps.
S0.quote: A faster list can show me the date, but it cannot make the festival book it.
fieldNote: His **senior band skill** earns a low seasonal fee despite a master's degree and long experience.
Occasional **AI travel drafts** are checked against signed bookings and a paper notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the festival a quicker travel list helps if it still carries the paid rehearsal and mileage. The mandolin tune needs a player who can watch the dancers turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The short season and three weeks saved make a cancelled festival set painful already. My partner's seasonal pay does not close the winter gap just because AI is mild.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll confirm five paid festival sets and three pupils, and ask the manager for written cancellation and travel fees. In the first year of this small change I'll keep checking occasional AI travel drafts against signed bookings and save one fifth of each extra cleared dance fee after rent, food and instrument repairs toward one month of expenses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the ordinary winter gap. A faster list can show me the date, but it cannot make the festival book it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the wet field?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A wet field cancelled a summer dance last year. The organiser paid our mileage but not the lost playing fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you check a travel list?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I check the hall and the last bus in a paper notebook. An AI list once put a school two stops past the signed address.

say: I'd ask which **paid part hours** software will replace.
I'd seek **separate fees** for band leading and preparation before another season.
think: Parts and plans bring **one-third** of my own musician pay.
Our **three-week reserve** cannot fund a winter search.
do: Compare **ten part invoices** and request a paid checker demonstration outside booked dances.
Test **AI notation checker** on owned nameless tune with festival-funded paid-use licence and approved local storage.
Play **each changed bar**; stop wrong notes/leaks and require written consent for others' audio.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic losses to preparation pay.
S1.quote: A clean score is not a paid dance.
fieldNote: His **new AI lesson** differs from occasional travel lists and requires paid time without displaced dances.
The **test tune** is owned, nameless and commercially permitted, with manual checks and storage stop rules.

steps.text: Compare ten part invoices; request paid notation-checker demo outside booked dances

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the festival which paid practice-part and route-planning hours its new software will replace. I'd ask for the band-leader and preparation fees on separate lines before signing next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those parts and plans bring about a third of my own pay. If the festival buys fewer, three weeks saved will not carry a winter search for a rare band-leader post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll compare ten paid part invoices with the festival's new order list and ask for a paid demonstration of a new AI notation checker, which flags written music errors. In the first year I'll test only a nameless tune I own under the festival's funded paid-use licence and approved local storage, playing each suggested bar against paper and stopping for wrong notes or leakage; I'll keep booked dances and pupils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a real cut to paid preparation. A clean score is not a paid dance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a pupil's recording?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A pupil's playing will not enter that test. I would need written permission and a clear storage rule before using anyone else's recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the checker lesson?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The festival must pay the instructor and not take a booked dance hour for training. If it asks me to buy the licence, I'll use the paper score.

S2.quote: A long music career does not tell me what the actual pension payment will be each month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could write practice parts before a robot plays mandolin. Playing robots follow around 2031, so our live festival calls need signing now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the festival to stop buying parts and route plans in 2028, taking a third of my pay. Live dances may also be cut later, but I will not count them lost while the current dates stand. I lie awake working out which bill could wait after that loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total part and planning fees, ask for signed paid festival calls and request actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if paid dances also fall, I'll seek a posted paid community ensemble-director role only if my master's and band-leading history qualify, actual live ensemble direction and teaching are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works; I'll keep the band and pupils until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about an expected third of my pay disappearing when we have three weeks saved. I can ask about an opening, but there are few nearby groups to ask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a director role open now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No community centre has offered me a director role. I would read a real paid posting and its hours before treating it as income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you stop at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have not seen the pension figures. A long music career does not tell me what the actual pension payment will be each month.

Use **own tunes** and require written school/family consent before recording children.
Repeat **after 2031** only if part fees fall and written paid room/sound/schedule terms hold; otherwise keep existing work.

S3.quote: A school hall full of children is not a wage unless the fee is signed.
fieldNote: His **second payer** is a school with a real signed performance fee, not an assumed teaching vacancy.
He **protects current calls** and requires written safe school equipment and consent for child recording.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the school arts office that five years to AGI by 2031 lets us price a paid live folk assembly, not a free demonstration. Playing robots follow around 2034, so I would ask for written human-player fees now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cheapen parts and route plans before 2031. A separate school performance could add income, but a principal's interest is not a paid booking and I cannot drop a festival rehearsal to chase it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll pitch two separate paid school folk assemblies only if the school signs a fee covering my playing, preparation and bus costs, commits in writing to a safe hall and sound equipment, and schedules them outside booked festival and pupil hours. I would use only my own tunes and not record children without written school and family permission. In the first year after 2031, if part fees fall, I'll repeat the assemblies only while those written paid, room, sound and schedule terms hold; without real signed dates I'll keep festival and pupil work and budget no school fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about fading part income, though a real second payer could help. A school hall full of children is not a wage unless the fee is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has a school agreed to pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No school has agreed to the assembly. An arts teacher asked what it costs, which is a question, not a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who checks the room and sound?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school must inspect its sound equipment and approve the room in writing. I will bring my own mandolin but not pay for a hall or an unsafe speaker.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my grown children that ten years to AGI by 2036 lets us get real pension figures and paid festival dates on paper. Mandolin-playing robots follow around 2039; the winter rent comes before then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need band and pupil fees. Three weeks saved now and an unknown pension do not make a stopping date safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid festival plan, then save ten percent of each extra cleared dance fee after rent, food and mandolin repairs toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid band and pupil work while booked and seek separate school assemblies only with signed playing/preparation/bus pay, written school provision of a safe room and sound, consent for recordings and no displaced calls; if live band pay falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted ensemble-director role only if my master's and leadership qualify, actual live ensemble direction and teaching are paid, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works, staying until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a long run of low seasonal pay. A decade gives me time to ask, not a pension amount in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra dance pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra dance fee clears, I save nothing from it. I will not move rent money just to show a larger reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen pension figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen the pension amount. I will compare the actual statement with winter bills before dropping a paid date.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because paid parts and plans could end before another senior band post opens. Signed festival dates, actual pension figures and a posted qualified director role with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many school assemblies pay a band leader after the bus home. A full school hall is not a paid folk show without a signed fee.

headlineQuote: A full school hall is not a paid folk show without a signed fee.
portrait: Aaron is a **58-year-old folk band leader** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
His **low seasonal pay**, three-week reserve and few nearby senior jobs persist despite excellent playing.
He uses **AI occasionally** for travel and learns a new checker only through paid, private and manually checked trials.
He seeks **separate paid school shows** only with signed fees, safe rooms and no displaced festival work.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove a third of Aaron's pay from parts and route plans.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed festival calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualified directing with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
